A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FOLK research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original FOLK experiments on ImageNet-1K and ADE20K, including classification, few-shot learning, segmentation, ablations and GPU memory measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds ViT-B evaluations, CNN few-shot results, CIFAR evaluations, corruption tests and further ablations.

M1.justification: Both versions retain adaptive Com/RCom masking, the EMA teacher/student architecture, projection heads and combined reconstruction/distillation objective. The default thresholds, equal filter-selection probability and loss weight remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents the existing filter-generation procedure.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained ImageNet-1K and ADE20K evaluations, v2 adds CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 evaluations in the threshold study (Table 8). It also introduces reconstruction tests under salt-and-pepper noise, Gaussian noise, brightness changes and contrast changes (Appendix B.3), expanding the represented input conditions.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes SimMIM, which had 80.9% ViT-S accuracy in v1. The segmentation comparison in Table 3 adds MFM + Com/RCom at 45.1 mIoU. Appendix C.4 also adds a numerical memory comparison against DINO using an attributed, batch-adjusted figure; the principal comparator sets otherwise remain stable.

E3.justification: v2 adds ViT-B/16 evaluations, ResNet-50 few-shot experiments, and few-shot results using 800 pre-training epochs, including a 1000-epoch fine-tuning condition for 10% labeled data. Its new corruption protocol evaluates reconstruction loss on 100 randomly selected validation images, with specified Gaussian noise and brightness/contrast perturbations. These extend the evaluation design rather than establish reruns of retained results.

E4.justification: v2 adds threshold-set sensitivity tests, Com/RCom selection-probability ablations, image-corruption tests and a controlled comparison of reconstruction-loss trajectories without self-distillation (Tables 6, 8, 9 and Figure 5). The existing loss-weight and alternative-filter ablations are retained as Tables 10 and 11; their relocation is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Averages across learning-rate configurations already appear in v1. The new average corruption losses and Gaussian-noise standard deviation do not provide uncertainty estimates for experimental outcomes.

E6.justification: Most matched original accuracies remain unchanged. New results include FOLK ViT-B accuracies of 83.4% and 84.0% after 300 and 800 pre-training epochs, ResNet-50 few-shot accuracies of 71.1% and 46.2% with 10% and 1% labels, and additional segmentation, corruption and sensitivity results. Tables 2 and 7 add longer-budget few-shot results rather than same-setting improvements. The new 84.0% ViT-B result equals the reported iBOT accuracy at a different pre-training budget.

T1.justification: The Fourier transform, masking, reconstruction loss, softmax, distillation loss, EMA update and combined objective remain mathematically unchanged, as does the appendix learning-rate formula. Neither version develops theorems or proofs. The added pseudocode makes existing procedural details explicit.

C1.justification: The abstract, three introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: adaptive frequency masking and self-distillation address MFM limitations and support competitive classification, few-shot learning and segmentation. The expanded evidence does not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B.2 newly acknowledges the absence of full-data CNN gains over MFM and proposes architectural inductive biases as an explanation, while emphasizing low-data benefits. New discussion attributes noise robustness to spatial-domain training, randomized masking and augmentation, and interprets the threshold and filter-probability studies as evidence of limited tuning sensitivity. These add substantive applicability qualifications and mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link and explicit percentile-based filter-generation pseudocode in Appendix A.4. It also clarifies iBOT result provenance, discloses pre-training budgets in the few-shot tables and specifies parameters for the new corruption tests. Most existing optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size, head and hardware details are retained.

R1.justification: New Section 3.2.4 and Appendix C make the distinctions from DINO, iBOT and AttMask explicit through masking domain, objectives, input views and resource comparisons. This elaborates the existing positioning around MFM and self-distillation. The cited-work set remains essentially unchanged; the BEiT year/venue change refers to the same work.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: semantic segmentation and loss-weight analysis move from the main text into Appendix B, ablations are regrouped, and a dedicated comparison appendix is inserted before the retained visualizations. Classification and few-shot discussions are rewritten, and the appendix gains a structured overview and more detailed subsection organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds four result tables, Algorithm 1 and the loss-trajectory Figure 5. Table 1 gains a ViT-B column, and few-shot tables gain MAX/Epoch columns and additional rows. Existing displays are relocated and reformatted within the ICLR layout, including shaded table headers. Figures 1–4 and the prediction examples are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central design: previously untested threshold and filter-selection choices receive targeted ablations, and CNN few-shot experiments clarify benefits that were obscured by v1's tied full-data CNN results. Larger-model evaluations and explicit filter pseudocode further improve validation and reproducibility. The gains are qualified by absent run-level uncertainty, sparse CIFAR setup details and corruption evidence limited to reconstruction on 100 images, but the targeted evidence resolves important gaps in v1.
